items.stem: What does mean corpuscular volume (MCV) measure?

options.A: The total number of circulating red blood cells in a measured blood volume.
options.B: The average size or volume of circulating red blood cells.
options.C: The average amount of hemoglobin contained in each red blood cell.
options.D: The percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells.

items.rationale: MCV stands for mean corpuscular volume and measures the average size of red blood cells. It is one of the red-cell indices used to help classify anemia.
items.locator: Definition of MCV as average red blood cell size

items.stem: A nurse is preparing to transfer a client from bed to wheelchair. Which action best reflects safe patient-handling practice?

options.A: Use a gait belt and perform a one-person transfer before determining whether the client can bear weight.
options.B: Manually lift the client’s full body weight when the transfer distance is short and a second nurse is nearby.
options.C: Assess the client’s mobility and assistance needs, then use appropriate assistive equipment and additional staff when indicated.
options.D: Begin the transfer without equipment, then add a device only if the client becomes unstable while standing.

items.rationale: NIOSH identifies patient handling as a major musculoskeletal-injury risk and recommends safe patient-handling and mobility strategies, including appropriate assistive lifting devices. Transfer planning should be based on the patient's mobility and assistance needs rather than routine manual lifting.
items.source_name: CDC/NIOSH — About Safe Patient Handling and Mobility
items.locator: Safe patient handling includes use of assistive lifting technology and appropriate procedures to reduce injury risk during lifting, moving, and repositioning.

items.stem: During admission, a nurse identifies a wound on a client's lower leg. Which documentation is most appropriate?

options.A: Record the wound stage and a photograph only; measurements and drainage characteristics can be added at discharge.
options.B: Record the dressing type and pain score only because wound-bed and surrounding-skin findings are treatment rather than assessment data.
options.C: Delay the baseline description until the first scheduled dressing change so admission findings do not affect later comparisons.
options.D: Record the wound’s precise location, size, wound-bed and periwound findings, drainage, pain, and other relevant assessment characteristics.

items.rationale: NCBI Nursing Skills specifies that wound assessment and documentation include anatomical location, wound type, tissue damage, wound bed, size, edges and periwound skin, signs of infection, pain, and drainage characteristics. Accurate baseline documentation supports ongoing comparison and care planning.
items.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Skills: Wound Care
items.locator: Wound assessment documentation includes precise location, size, wound characteristics, periwound findings, drainage, infection findings, and pain.

items.stem: An older adult takes twelve medications prescribed by several clinicians. Which concern should the nurse prioritize during medication review?

options.A: Review the complete medication regimen, including prescription drugs, OTC products, and supplements, for adverse effects, interactions, duplication, and management problems.
options.B: Review only medications prescribed by the admitting clinician because drugs from other prescribers are outside the current medication review.
options.C: Stop the oldest medications first because duration of therapy is the primary criterion for deprescribing in polypharmacy.
options.D: Assume the regimen is safe when every drug was prescribed by a licensed clinician, even when several prescribers are involved.

items.rationale: The National Institute on Aging identifies polypharmacy as a particular concern in older adults. Taking many medicines can increase the risk of adverse reactions, drug interactions, and medication-management difficulties, making comprehensive review important.
items.source_name: National Institute on Aging — Taking Medicines Safely as You Age
items.locator: Polypharmacy/medication management: maintain and review a complete list because multiple medicines increase adverse-effect and interaction risk.

items.stem: Which home-safety teaching is appropriate for an older adult at risk for falls?

options.A: Limit routine walking inside the home so the older adult has fewer opportunities to experience a fall.
options.B: Remove tripping hazards, improve lighting, and install bathroom grab bars or other appropriate home-safety supports.
options.C: Keep familiar throw rugs in walking paths while adding brighter lighting to improve visual contrast.
options.D: Use loose backless slippers indoors because they are easier to remove if balance is lost.

items.rationale: CDC fall-prevention guidance recommends removing trip hazards, improving home lighting, and installing grab bars near the toilet and tub or shower. These measures directly reduce common environmental fall hazards.
items.source_name: CDC — Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures
items.locator: CDC home-safety recommendations include removing trip hazards, adding grab bars, and improving lighting.

items.stem: Which statement should a nurse include when teaching an adult about motor-vehicle injury prevention?

options.A: Reserve seat-belt use mainly for highway travel because short local trips have minimal serious-injury risk.
options.B: Adults seated in the rear seat can omit seat belts when the vehicle has front and side airbags.
options.C: Wear a seat belt on every trip because consistent restraint use substantially reduces the risk of serious crash-related injury or death.
options.D: Seat belts are primarily a pediatric intervention and add little protection after a passenger reaches adulthood.

items.rationale: CDC states that seat belts are the most effective way to prevent injury or death in crashes for adults and older children and that they reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. Consistent use on every trip is recommended.
items.source_name: CDC — Facts About Seat Belt Use
items.locator: Seat belts reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths and should be used on every trip.

items.stem: A parent asks how to protect a 4-month-old infant from ultraviolet exposure. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Use sunscreen as the primary protection for the infant because shade and clothing provide insufficient ultraviolet protection.
options.B: Provide brief direct midday sun exposure each day because infants younger than 6 months are less susceptible to sunburn.
options.C: Apply an adult sunscreen routinely to all exposed skin before using shade or protective clothing.
options.D: Keep the 4-month-old out of direct sunlight when possible, use shade and protective clothing, and ask the pediatrician before applying sunscreen.

items.rationale: FDA guidance recommends keeping infants younger than 6 months out of direct sunlight, using shade and protective clothing, and consulting a pediatrician before applying sunscreen to this age group. Sunscreen is not generally recommended as the primary protection for young infants.
items.source_name: FDA — Should You Put Sunscreen on Infants? Not Usually
items.locator: For infants younger than 6 months, FDA recommends shade and protective clothing and advises consulting a pediatrician before sunscreen use.

items.stem: What is the purpose of Mental Health First Aid training for community members?

options.A: Teach community members to recognize mental-health or substance-use challenges, provide initial support, and help connect the person with appropriate care.
options.B: Teach community members to diagnose psychiatric disorders and select definitive treatment plans independently.
options.C: Train nonclinicians to replace professional services by providing ongoing psychotherapy and medication management.
options.D: Teach participants to avoid responding until a licensed clinician is physically present.

items.rationale: Mental Health First Aid teaches participants to recognize signs of mental health or substance-use challenges, provide initial support, and help connect people with appropriate professional care. The program explicitly does not train participants to diagnose or replace professional treatment.
items.source_name: Mental Health First Aid USA — Frequently Asked Questions
items.locator: MHFA teaches recognition, response, first-level support, and connection to appropriate care; First Aiders do not diagnose or replace professional help.

items.stem: A client with PTSD begins experiencing a flashback during an assessment. Which nursing response is most appropriate initially?

options.A: Ask for a detailed narrative of the traumatic event while the flashback is occurring so the memory can be processed immediately.
options.B: Speak calmly and use simple grounding cues that orient the client to the present situation and current surroundings.
options.C: Leave the client alone until the episode ends because interaction generally prolongs trauma-related flashbacks.
options.D: Challenge the accuracy of the traumatic memory during the flashback to help the client distinguish it from current reality.

items.rationale: The VA National Center for PTSD describes grounding as a strategy for intrusive thoughts and flashbacks that helps the person focus on the current situation rather than the traumatic event. Calm, simple present-focused orientation is appropriate; detailed trauma processing is not the immediate goal during an acute flashback.
items.source_name: VA National Center for PTSD — Grounding Technique
items.locator: Grounding for intrusive thoughts/flashbacks: focus attention on the current situation and present sensory surroundings.

items.stem: A hospitalized client with heavy alcohol use develops severe tremor, confusion, hallucinations, and marked autonomic hyperactivity after stopping alcohol. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Hepatic encephalopathy, which is established by tremor and hallucinations after abrupt alcohol cessation without further evaluation.
options.B: Wernicke encephalopathy, which is defined by marked autonomic hyperactivity and hallucinations after stopping alcohol.
options.C: Alcohol withdrawal delirium, a severe withdrawal syndrome requiring prompt medical treatment and close monitoring.
options.D: A primary psychotic disorder, which is more likely than withdrawal when severe tremor and autonomic hyperactivity follow alcohol cessation.

items.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal delirium is a severe withdrawal syndrome characterized by delirium with autonomic hyperactivity and can include hallucinations and marked tremor. It is medically dangerous and requires prompt treatment and monitoring rather than reassurance alone.
items.source_name: American Society of Addiction Medicine — Alcohol Withdrawal Management Guideline
items.locator: Alcohol withdrawal delirium: severe withdrawal with delirium/autonomic activation; recommendations VI.7–VI.13 address close monitoring and active medical management.
items.version: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline 2020 remains the active ASAM alcohol-withdrawal guideline; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
